subject: Chemistry
description: Catalysis basics: types of catalysts (positive, negative, auto-, biological), characteristics, industrial applications, enzyme catalysis.

questions.stem: What is the primary effect of a CATALYST in a chemical reaction?

options.option_text: It changes the rate of reaction
It increases the yield of products.

questions.explanation: A CATALYST changes the RATE (speed) of a reaction without being consumed. KEY MECHANISM: it lowers the ACTIVATION ENERGY (Ea) by providing an alternative reaction pathway — both forward and reverse rates speed up equally, so equilibrium POSITION does NOT change (only equilibrium is REACHED FASTER). KEY DISTINCTIONS: (1) Catalyst does NOT change ΔG, ΔH, or Keq — these are state functions of reactants/products. (2) Catalyst does NOT increase YIELD — yield depends on equilibrium position. (3) Catalyst does NOT get consumed — it can theoretically work indefinitely (in practice, deactivates over time via poisoning or sintering). TYPES: POSITIVE (speeds up; e.g., Pt in Haber process), NEGATIVE/inhibitor (slows down; e.g., glycerol slows hydrogen-peroxide decomposition), AUTO (a product catalyses its own formation; e.g., MnSO₄ in KMnO₄-oxalate reaction), BIOLOGICAL (enzymes; e.g., amylase, pepsin). INDUSTRIAL: 90% of all manufactured chemicals use catalysts at some stage. PYQ ANGLE: definitional Qs on catalysts appear in 80% of SSC CGL papers.

questions.stem: Which catalyst is used in the Haber process for ammonia synthesis?
questions.explanation: HABER-BOSCH PROCESS: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃; catalyst = finely-divided IRON with molybdenum (Mo) or aluminium oxide (Al₂O₃) as PROMOTER (a substance that enhances catalyst activity). Conditions: 200 atm pressure, 450-500°C. NOBEL: Fritz Haber 1918 (synthesis); Carl Bosch 1931 (industrial scale-up). HISTORICAL IMPACT: Haber process feeds ~50% of humanity by enabling synthetic nitrogen fertilizer — without it, world food output would crash. INDIA: India's largest urea producer is IFFCO (Indian Farmers Fertiliser Cooperative); urea is produced by reacting ammonia with CO₂. RELATED CATALYSTS — memorize: Contact process (H₂SO₄ from SO₂) → V₂O₅; Hydrogenation of oils → finely-divided Ni; Ostwald process (HNO₃ from NH₃) → Pt-Rh gauze; CO oxidation in catalytic converters (cars) → Pt-Pd-Rh. EXAM ANGLE: HABER + CONTACT + OSTWALD catalysts trio appears as a 3-mark MCQ in 80% of SSC CGL/RRB papers. EXAMINER MINDSET: testing memorization of industrial chemistry catalysts — direct PYQ recall.

questions.stem: Enzymes are biological catalysts made primarily of:
questions.explanation: ENZYMES are PROTEINS (with a few RNA exceptions called RIBOZYMES, e.g., self-splicing RNA in some viruses). They speed up biochemical reactions by ~10⁶ to 10¹² times via the LOCK-AND-KEY (or induced-fit) mechanism — the substrate binds to the enzyme's ACTIVE SITE. KEY PROPERTIES: (1) HIGHLY SPECIFIC — one enzyme typically catalyses one reaction (amylase only on starch, lipase only on fats). (2) SENSITIVE to pH and temperature — denatured by extremes (above ~50°C most human enzymes die). (3) Reusable — not consumed. EXAMPLES: amylase (starch → maltose; in saliva, pancreas), pepsin (proteins → peptides; stomach pH ~2), trypsin (small intestine pH ~8), catalase (H₂O₂ → H₂O + O₂; in liver/blood — the fastest known enzyme, 40 million reactions/sec). NOBEL TRIVIA: 2014 chemistry prize for super-resolution microscopy revealed enzyme dynamics at sub-diffraction scale. INDIA: enzymatic stain-removers (Surf Excel, Tide) use bacterial proteases sourced from Indian soil microbes.

options.option_text: A product catalyzes its own formation

questions.explanation: AUTOCATALYSIS: a PRODUCT of the reaction acts as the catalyst for its own further formation — so the reaction starts slow, then SPEEDS UP as more product accumulates, then slows again as reactants deplete. CLASSIC EXAMPLE: oxalic acid (H₂C₂O₄) + KMnO₄ in acidic medium produces Mn²⁺ (Mn(II)), which then catalyses the same reaction. The titration is initially slow, then speeds up — indicator of autocatalysis. RATE CURVE: S-shaped (sigmoidal) instead of standard exponential decay. BIOLOGICAL ANALOGS: pepsinogen → pepsin auto-activation in stomach; blood-clotting cascade has autocatalytic loops; cancer cell-cycle has autocatalytic feedback (one of the reasons tumours grow exponentially). INDUSTRIAL: certain polymerization reactions (e.g., styrene) are autocatalytic — controlled carefully to avoid runaway exotherms. PYQ ANGLE: autocatalysis vs catalysis vs inhibition appears as a definition-MCQ in JEE-Main and SSC CGL Tier 2. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests conceptual depth beyond rote 'what is a catalyst'.

questions.stem: In the Contact Process for sulphuric acid manufacture, which catalyst converts SO₂ to SO₃?
questions.explanation: CONTACT PROCESS: S → SO₂ (burn S in air) → SO₃ (oxidation, catalysed by V₂O₅) → H₂SO₄ (dissolve in conc. H₂SO₄ to form oleum, then dilute with water). The KEY catalytic step is 2SO₂ + O₂ → 2SO₃ at 400-450°C with V₂O₅ catalyst. WHY V₂O₅? Originally Pt was used (faster, but expensive and easily POISONED by arsenic impurities in the SO₂ feed). V₂O₅ is cheaper, robust, less prone to poisoning. INDUSTRIAL SCALE: H₂SO₄ is the world's #1 industrial chemical (~250 million tonnes/year); ~85% goes to fertilizer (phosphate), rest to detergents, dyes, pickling steel. INDIAN INDUSTRY: India produces ~10 million tonnes H₂SO₄ annually; major plants at Tuticorin, Gujarat (GACL, GNFC). HISTORICAL: Contact process patented by Peregrine Phillips (UK, 1831) — but commercialized properly only in 1900s. PYQ TRIO: V₂O₅ for Contact, Fe for Haber, Pt-Rh for Ostwald — these three appear together in 70%+ SSC Chemistry MCQs.

options.option_text: A poison made by the catalyst.

questions.explanation: A CATALYTIC POISON is a substance that DEACTIVATES a catalyst by binding strongly to its active sites, blocking reactant access. EXAMPLES: (1) ARSENIC compounds poison platinum in Contact process — that's why V₂O₅ is preferred industrially. (2) LEAD poisons the platinum-rhodium catalytic converter in cars — that's why leaded petrol was banned globally (in India, 2000). (3) SULPHUR poisons nickel in hydrogenation reactions — feedstocks must be desulphurized first. (4) CARBON MONOXIDE poisons iron in Haber process — H₂ feed must be purified. (5) MERCURY poisons many enzyme catalysts (and biological enzymes — hence Hg toxicity). DIFFERENT FROM INHIBITOR: an inhibitor reversibly slows reaction; a poison usually irreversibly destroys catalyst. INDUSTRIAL CONSEQUENCE: catalyst replacement is a major cost; refineries spend ~$100M/year on catalyst regeneration globally. ENVIRONMENTAL: catalytic converters last ~100,000 km if leaded fuel/poor maintenance avoided; replacement costs ₹15-30k. PYQ ANGLE: 'why was leaded petrol banned' = catalytic poison + Pb-toxicity dual-answer.

questions.stem: What term describes a catalyst in the SAME phase (e.g., liquid + liquid) as the reactants?
questions.explanation: HOMOGENEOUS CATALYSIS — catalyst and reactants in SAME phase (both gases, or both liquids, or both solutions). EXAMPLE: acid-catalyzed esterification (CH₃COOH + C₂H₅OH → ester + H₂O), where H⁺ from H₂SO₄ is in the same liquid solution. HETEROGENEOUS CATALYSIS — different phases (catalyst usually solid, reactants gas/liquid). EXAMPLE: solid V₂O₅ in Contact process catalysing gas-phase SO₂ + O₂. PROS/CONS: heterogeneous = easier separation/recovery (filter or fixed bed), used in 90% of industrial chemistry; homogeneous = better selectivity, single-step, but harder catalyst recovery. SURFACE CATALYSIS THEORY: heterogeneous catalysis works via ADSORPTION on the catalyst surface (Langmuir-Hinshelwood mechanism). NOBEL: Gerhard Ertl (2007) for fundamentals of surface chemistry / heterogeneous catalysis (Haber process mechanism). PHASE-TRANSFER CATALYSIS: a catalyst (often quaternary ammonium salt) ferries reactants between two immiscible phases — used in pharmaceutical synthesis. PYQ FREQUENCY: homo vs hetero catalysis is a 1-mark MCQ in JEE-Main and rare in SSC.
